Tortuous

TOR-choo-us -- from Latin tortuosus, from torquere ('to twist'). Not to be confused with the similar-sounding torturous ('extremely painful'). · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Tortuous is full of twists and turns; excessively winding or complicated.

The spelunkers followed a tortuous path deep into the cave system, doubling back through the same narrow passage twice.

Worked Example

What should have been a simple permit request turned into a tortuous process involving six different offices and eleven separate forms.

That winding, needlessly complicated path -- whether a literal road or a bureaucratic process -- with far more twists than the destination requires is exactly what tortuous describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

winding: having many bends and turns

tangled: twisted together in a confused, complicated way

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

straightforward: simple and easy to understand or follow

direct: going straight to a point, without detours

Where it sits · how hard it is to follow — winding → tortuous → tangled

winding vs. tortuous: A winding trail led up through the pines to the overlook.

tangled vs. tortuous: Tangled is stronger than tortuous: tortuous instructions twist and wander but can still be followed, while tangled ones are so knotted together that even the technician gave up and called for help.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — tort-

root — tort-: to twist (Latin (torquere))

suffix — -uous

suffix — -uous: full of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Tortuous comes from Latin torquere, 'to twist,' plus -uous ('full of') -- something tortuous is literally full of twists, whether a winding road or an endlessly complicated process.

Use the root in a new word: contort

Word Choice

Watch the spelling closely: tortuous (winding, complicated) is easy to confuse with the similar-sounding torturous (extremely painful, like torture) -- they share the same Latin root but mean genuinely different things today.
